solution: Kid i is jealous of j_i and likes l_i, and an order is safe iff for every i either pos[j_i] < pos[i] or pos[i] < pos[l_i] < pos[j_i]; so each kid picks one of two precedence-edge sets -- j_i -> i, or the pair i -> l_i and l_i -> j_i -- and any topological order of an acyclic union is an answer. Because j_i < i for i >= 2, the jealousy map is an out-degree-1 functional graph: a tree rooted at kid 1 plus one back edge, so if every kid starts on the first option the only cycle is the root path 1..j_1 together with that edge. At least one kid on that cycle must be flipped to the second option; flipping v deletes j_v -> v and adds v -> l_v and l_v -> j_v, which produces a fresh cycle exactly when j_v can still reach l_v down the tree (l_v a descendant of j_v along an unbroken path), and that smaller cycle is resolved by the same rule recursively. Branching over the still-cuttable edges of the current cycle is complete -- every solution must delete one of them -- so correctness of both the order and the 'impossible' verdict follows, which is what the brute force confirms. Each search node is one O(n) pass and only touches its own cycle, whose edges are never revisited deeper; with DFS numbering plus a structure for the 'still reachable' test the intended implementation is O(n) to O(n log n), and in testing the search never exceeded 9 nodes, so n = 200000 is comfortable (0.4 s even in Python).
statement_summary: Each of n kids is jealous of one other kid and likes another; everyone except the coolest envies someone cooler, so the jealousy relation is a tree plus one extra edge. A kid may misbehave if the envied kid goes later and the liked kid does not go strictly in between. With n up to 200000, a safe order must be produced, or impossibility reported.

Verification: verify_kindergarten2.py checks both official samples (sample 1 answers 4 1 2 3, another valid order than the judge's 1 2 3 4, which the statement allows; sample 2 -> impossible), then agrees with a permutation brute force on all 292 instances with n = 3,4 and with a 2^n option-assignment brute force on all 23328 instances with n = 5, plus 30000 random instances at n = 6..10 over random / star / chain / narrow trees -- zero mismatches. Impossible instances are rare (130 of 23328 at n = 5) but real. Labels: graph-modeling is the crux (turning 'no surprise' into a two-way choice of precedence edges); topological-sort produces the output; functional-graph is the tree-plus-one-cycle structure of the jealousy map that makes the cycle unique and the search small. binary-search-answer, dp-on-dag and greedy do NOT apply. tin-tout-ancestor-check is kept at 0.5 only: the pivot test really is 'is l_v a descendant of j_v', but a linear implementation needs a dynamic version of it (current root per vertex over DFS ranges, e.g. an ordered map of contiguous ranges or a segment tree) rather than a static tin/tout compare. Uncertainty: my branching search is provably complete but only exponential-worst-case in theory; the published linear implementation (Bruce Merry's WF 2024 write-up, which matches the structure derived here) is explicitly stated by its author to lack a completeness proof, so 'this exact recursion is linear on every input' is the one claim I cannot back.
